questions.question: What is a sample in a field study?
choices: Every organism on Earth
Only the final written conclusion
An instrument used to measure wind
A subset of the population or area being studied

questions.question: What is a quadrat commonly used for?
choices: Counting all organisms over an entire region at once
Sampling organisms within a defined area
Measuring only the age of each sampled organism
Collecting observations only along a single line

questions.question: What is a transect?
choices: A randomly chosen square sampling area
The total organisms counted at one point
A line or path along which observations are collected
A tool used only to measure soil acidity

questions.question: What is random sampling intended to reduce?
choices: Bias from choosing sites based on preference
Natural differences among all organisms
The need for any repeat sampling
All uncertainty in the final population estimate

questions.question: What is stratified sampling?
choices: Sampling only the easiest location to reach
Sampling within defined subgroups or habitat sections
Sampling only the largest individuals
Recording no location information

questions.question: What is a field notebook used for?
choices: Recording observations, methods, times, and locations
Recording only results that match the prediction
Replacing the original observations with a final opinion
Listing equipment without recording observations

questions.question: What is sampling bias?
choices: Ordinary variation among organisms
The average of repeated measurements
A sampling process that systematically favors some members or conditions
A difference caused only by random rounding

questions.question: Why should the same sampling method be used when comparing two sites?
choices: It guarantees the sites are identical
It removes every environmental variable
It prevents all organisms from moving
It makes differences less likely to result from method changes

questions.question: Why can studying only roadside plants misrepresent a whole forest?
choices: Roadside plants automatically represent every habitat equally
Roadside conditions may differ from the forest interior
Forest interior conditions cannot affect plant distributions
Only plant size, never sampling location, affects estimates

questions.question: Why should field researchers record weather and season?
choices: These records replace the need to count organisms
Season affects only the observer, not organisms
Weather information proves the hypothesis without data
These conditions can influence observations and species activity

questions.question: Why can repeated visits improve a wildlife survey?
choices: Detectability and activity can vary over time
Repeated visits guarantee detection of every species
One visit always represents every time of day
Detectability is identical for all species and seasons

questions.question: Why should researchers minimize disturbance during surveys?
choices: Disturbance always improves the original habitat estimate
A survey's presence cannot affect organism behavior
Disturbance can harm organisms and alter what is being measured
The most reliable survey removes every organism

questions.question: Why does a larger representative sample usually improve an estimate?
choices: It guarantees an exact count of all individuals
It compensates completely for biased site selection
It reduces the influence of chance variation in small samples
It removes the need to record variation

questions.question: Why are individual quadrat counts retained instead of recording only their total?
choices: They reveal variation between sampled locations
Totals alone show every location's variation
A mean cannot be calculated from individual counts
Each quadrat must have the same count

questions.question: Why should sampling locations be documented?
choices: Coordinates replace all details of the sampling method
Recording locations prevents habitats from changing
Only the date matters when repeating a field study
Other researchers can assess and repeat the sampling design

questions.question: Four equal quadrats contain 2, 4, 6, and 8 plants. What is the mean count per quadrat?
A 1 m² quadrat sample averages 3 plants, and the sampled habitat is 100 m². What is an estimated total if the sample is representative?
choices: 300 plants
30 plants
103 plants
3 plants

questions.question: A pond has vegetated and open-water sections. Which design best ensures both are represented?
choices: Sample only near the easiest access point
Sample only where the most fish are visible
Sample randomly within each section
Sample only the open-water section

questions.question: Two observers count birds at different times using different observation lengths. What is a major comparison problem?
choices: Observer identity is the only possible source of difference
Time and effort differ along with the observers
Different observation lengths guarantee equal effort
Time of day never affects bird detectability

questions.question: A survey finds no owls during one midday visit. What is the most defensible conclusion?
choices: The habitat certainly contains no owls
All owls have left the region permanently
The survey proves owls are extinct
No owls were detected during that visit
